question.question: v4
question.asks: Will NVIDIA disclose in its quarterly results or FY2027 Form 10-K that Vera Rubin made volume customer shipments with first revenue recognition by the end of FY2027 (January 31, 2027)?
question.settles_on: Whether Vera Rubin moves from full production to volume customer shipments and first revenue recognition within NVIDIA's fiscal 2027, as shown in the company's quarterly results and Form 10-K.

possible_answers.label: Yes
possible_answers.holds_when: NVIDIA's quarterly results or FY2027 Form 10-K show that Vera Rubin made volume customer shipments with first revenue recognition by January 31, 2027.

possible_answers.label: Ruled out
possible_answers.holds_when: After September 23, 2026, NVIDIA formally cancels or abandons the Vera Rubin platform before it makes volume customer shipments. This rung holds when that, or any other decision against the event of rung 1 as a whole, or a formal abandonment or withdrawal of it as a whole, was made after 2026-09-23 and stands on 2027-01-31, and only when rung 1 does not.

possible_answers.label: Still open
possible_answers.holds_when: Neither rung 1 nor rung 2 holds on 2027-01-31.

what_the_judge_was_shown:
Thesis v4 (NVDA, asset, focus "Whether Vera Rubin moves from full production to volume customer shipments and first revenue recognition within NVIDIA's fiscal 2027, as shown in the company's quarterly results and Form 10-K.", 2027, due 2027-01-31): Will NVIDIA disclose in its quarterly results or FY2027 Form 10-K that Vera Rubin made volume customer shipments with first revenue recognition by the end of FY2027 (January 31, 2027)?
Ladder: rung 1 Yes: NVIDIA's quarterly results or FY2027 Form 10-K show that Vera Rubin made volume customer shipments with first revenue recognition by January 31, 2027. / rung 2 Ruled out: After September 23, 2026, NVIDIA formally cancels or abandons the Vera Rubin platform before it makes volume customer shipments. This rung holds when that, or any other decision against the event of rung 1 as a whole, or a formal abandonment or withdrawal of it as a whole, was made after 2026-09-23 and stands on 2027-01-31, and only when rung 1 does not. / rung 3 Still open: Neither rung 1 nor rung 2 holds on 2027-01-31.

articles.title: Sea to adopt Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform; more Southeast Asian firms build with Nemotron
articles.text:
Sea to adopt Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform; more Southeast Asian firms build with Nemotron
Sea will use Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform to scale AI across Shopee, Monee and Garena, while organisations in Southeast Asia build applications with Nvidia's Nemotron models.
Singapore-founded Sea will adopt Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform to build and deploy artificial-intelligence (AI) models and agents at greater scale across its Shopee, Monee and Garena businesses.
Vera Rubin is a computing platform that provides the processing capacity to develop and run AI systems. Sea says it will use Vera Rubin to extend AI work already underway at its businesses.
At Shopee, Compass is an in-house AI model built and run on Nvidia graphics processors and software. It powers search, product recommendations, fraud checks and customer service.
Over eight months, Compass's monthly processing volume rose from 3 billion to 340 billion tokens. Tokens are the units of text an AI model reads and generates. Compass now accounts for most of Shopee's AI traffic. It has also made fraud detection 50 times more efficient than manual review and cut processing costs by 90%.
Beyond Compass, Shopee uses AI to help sellers create product listings, improve product discovery, and engage customers.
Meanwhile, Sea's digital-financial-services division Monee uses AI to detect fraud and assess credit risk. As for Garena, it uses AI to improve gaming experiences and support safe, inclusive online spaces.
Another Nvidia offering seeing an uptake in Southeast Asia is Nemotron, which is a collection of open AI models, datasets and software tools that organisations can customise for their own languages and business needs.
For instance, NCS has adopted Nemotron models and its video-search-and-summarisation blueprint for enterprise and public-sector work. NCS is also developing physical-AI applications for humanoid robotics.
At ST Engineering, Nvidia's NeMo tools and cuOpt software are being used to develop its AI Studio platform and deploy AI applications in areas including marine maintenance, repair and overhaul.
Meanwhile, Singapore's Home Team Science and Technology Agency (HTX) is beginning research using two Nemotron models for public-safety applications. One model could support reasoning and agentic workflows, while the other combines vision, audio and language capabilities for applications based on operational data.
Other projects focus on adapting AI for local languages and legal systems. This includes AI Singapore adding Nemotron open models and NeMo tools to SEA-LION, its model family for Southeast Asian languages and cultures.
In Vietnam, Viettel AI has fine-tuned Nemotron 3 Super for Vietnamese-language and agentic applications. The model is set to be used in Legal AI, an agent system for Viettel Group employees and external customers.
Meanwhile, Thailand's iApp Technology is adapting Nemotron 3 Nano for Thai-language legal work. Nvidia says the resulting model powers Thanoy, iApp's legal-assistant chatbot, which serves about 43,000 users.
Nvidia also cites smart-city projects in the region. Malaysia's ITMAX is applying Nvidia software to traffic operations, while Thailand's AS-TECH is using it to improve passenger flow in airports.

articles.title: Sea doubles down on full-stack AI with Nvidia Vera Rubin
articles.text:
Sea doubles down on full-stack AI with Nvidia Vera Rubin
The Singapore-founded company, set to be Southeast Asia’s first enterprise to adopt Nvidia’s latest AI platform, runs its own datacentre infrastructure and models while equipping frontline teams with tools to build AI agents
Sea Group will be the first enterprise in Southeast Asia to adopt Nvidia’s Vera Rubin platform , building on an artificial intelligence (AI) strategy that lets it run every layer of its technology stack except the chips.
Speaking at Nvidia AI Day Singapore, Li Kuangli, senior director of partnerships and strategy at Sea, said the group is becoming “a full-stack AI company”.
“We see this as a core differentiator in how we choose to compete and create value in the AI era,” he said.
Garena, the gaming arm of Sea, has about 660 million quarterly active users across more than 160 markets, according to Li. Shopee has more than 400 million annual active buyers who place over 15 billion orders a year, while Sea’s digital financial services unit, Monee, has more than 40 million active credit users and a loan book of more than $11bn.
“Even a small improvement in how people access our products and services through AI can make a meaningful difference at this scale,” said Li.
Borrowing the “five-layer cake” analogy Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang often uses to describe the AI industry, Li called Sea’s version the “five-layer AI kueh lapis” after the layered cake popular in the region. It differs in putting chips rather than energy at the base and adding a platform layer between applications and models.
“Since we’re a Singaporean company and we consider Southeast Asia our home, we’ve adapted this five-layer AI cake into something a little more familiar to local tastebuds,” he said.
Sea does not make its own AI chips. It bought its first Nvidia accelerators in 2018 for its machine learning teams, has invested in every generation since Volta and was Southeast Asia’s first customer for Nvidia’s DGX A100 system . The ties go back to 2013, when Garena and Nvidia co-hosted campus League of Legends tournaments in Taiwan. More recently, both companies invested in world model startups World Labs and AMI Labs.
The companies said Vera Rubin, which combines Nvidia’s Vera central processing unit (CPU) with its Rubin graphics processing units (GPUs), will allow Sea to build and deploy AI models and agents at a larger scale. They did not say how big the deployment will be, or when it will go live.
On top of the chips is infrastructure that Sea runs itself: over 150,000 servers and more than 25,000 GPUs across 40-plus datacentres worldwide, with a combined critical IT load in excess of 100MW. The network has more than 120 interconnections with tier-one internet service providers, and handles over 1.1 exabytes of traffic a month – about 700 million hours of high-definition video, by Li’s calculations. Once the colocation partners have handed over the space, Sea’s teams take over design, procurement, deployment, testing, commissioning and operations.
“This is probably one of the less well-known capabilities that Sea has built up over time to support the immense scale and the rapid growth of our digital businesses,” said Li.
Sea pre-trains its own models, among them the Compass large language model (LLM), and has built specialised models for image and video generation. It also uses third-party models where they are suitable for the task and adapts open models for its needs. Li said an e-commerce LLM needs to understand product attributes, local languages and how shoppers express intent in their own marketplace.
“The right choice of model is driven by pragmatic considerations,” he said.
Teams reach these models through a shared gateway that enables applications to choose the model that best fits the job, with built-in deployment, usage and budget controls.
Sea has built its own platforms to put AI in employees’ hands. Alpha Intelligence is a graphical workflow, chatbot and agent builder. SeaTalk Spark is an AI agent embedded in the SeaTalk employee messaging app that summarises discussions, drafts replies and hands off work to other agents.
Smart connects AI agents to Sea’s business systems so teams can build and deploy agents with permissions, logs and cost tracking already in place.
One of those agents was built by SPX Express, Sea’s logistics arm. The company’s frontline team in Malaysia was manually checking delivery drivers’ fuel claims, so only a sample – less than 1% – was ever reviewed. The team used Smart to develop an agent that scans receipts, extracts details, checks them against policy and flags duplicates or claims for the wrong period before a human signs off.
“What is most amazing about this is that the business team was able to build this fully functional AI agent in less than two weeks using the common AI building blocks provided by Smart, with zero central developer resources needed,” said Li.
On Shopee, AI agents handle over 80% of customer queries without hurting customer satisfaction, he said. Sellers without a budget for a professional shoot can turn a basic photo into a better product image or an image and description into a short video, which Sea has found lifts engagement and conversions. Monee applies AI to fraud detection and credit risk assessment, according to the companies.
Garena, the business Sea started with, is researching game worlds populated by AI characters with their own personalities. Li showed a year-old internal demo in which a player asked for apples to rain down in a circle, and the scene was generated on the fly.
“If you squint in the corner, you can see it’s actually running on a very old model,” he said. “It’s on GPT-4.1, but it’s the only video that was allowed to show on stage.”
Li said Sea’s ownership of the stack lets it tailor AI to its markets and switch between in-house and outside technology as the frontier moves. “Having a common AI technology stack allows value to compound across the group,” he added.
Raymond Teh, senior vice-president for Asia-Pacific at Nvidia, opened the event by saying customers could purchase a single layer of Nvidia’s stack, or part of one, and combine it with technology from other suppliers.
“For government organisations running sovereign AI , this is a perfect example,” said Teh. “They can take the best in class of every area in this five-layer cake, and then create their own sovereign AI to drive and preserve the national language, the national culture, the national services for its citizens, and deploy through its national cloud, not foreign cloud.”
Marc Hamilton, vice-president of solutions architecture and engineering at Nvidia, showed GitHub data in which new repositories had climbed to 20 million a month by April, which he attributed to the growing use of coding agents . Those agents can run thousands of inferences on a single task, and some AI-native companies burnt through their annual coding budgets in the first month or two of this year, he said.
“In Silicon Valley today, when you’re applying for a job, one of the first questions is not what stock am I going to get: how much money are you going to pay me,” said Hamilton. “One of the first questions I get when I interview engineers: what is my token budget going to be?”
Speaking on a panel about taking AI from pilots to production, Denise Ang, chief strategy officer and director of AI Central at the Home Team Science and Technology Agency (HTX), said pilots often stall because they are run as technology projects – solutions looking for a problem. The other problem is ownership. A tech team builds the tool and consults the business, but once the pilot ends, nobody takes it further.
Instead, HTX begins with mission-related problems, and product squads work with Home Team departments from day one. One result is an AI copilot on kiosks in police stations to enable the public to file police reports. Ang remembered a job candidate who opened his interview by complimenting it. His father had been scammed, and the copilot had made it less painful to report.
“Can you imagine getting positive customer satisfaction feedback in the middle of an interview?” she said.
HTX also maintains a governance playbook and conducts risk checks before any AI system goes live. “When product teams know that there are guardrails in place, they actually have the confidence to deploy solutions faster,” said Ang.
Chang Sau Sheong, deputy chief executive at Singapore’s Government Technology Agency (GovTech), said measuring the value of AI is one of the hardest parts of the job, particularly in government, where the aim is to serve citizens rather than make money. Metrics must be agreed by all stakeholders. Then there is customer satisfaction.
“If you survey people who love your product, then you get very high scores, and generally product teams ended up doing that,” he said. GovTech also tracks adoption and usage against its actual user base.
Chang said there was “some grain of truth” in the view that Singapore, which cannot compete on the number of chips or people, could compete on governance. Because AI is less predictable than traditional software, evaluations will matter more, he said. He also wants Singapore to apply AI where it already excels, such as aviation, finance and healthcare.
“I don’t think we need to be good in everything because it’s going to be impossible,” he said.
APAC enterprises are consuming more tokens even as unit prices fall, and the advice on what to do about it runs from smarter caching and gated model access to renting their own infrastructure.
Bumrungrad International Hospital is using Salesforce’s Agentforce to summarise and route patient correspondence , with automated appointment booking and voice agents on the cards.
DBS has strung together as many as 80 agents to prepare credit approvals for big corporate clients but says the industry’s ability to police such systems is advancing at a fraction of the pace of the technology itself .
At Boomi World Tour Sydney, Brickworks, Bakers Delight and Cochlear explain how they are shoring up the integration, data and governance foundations that AI agents depend on .
Giuseppe Manai, partner for open innovation at NCS’s AI Central unit, said the IT services firm is working on physical AI use cases such as robots that talk to members of the public, and on the operating “fabric” needed to run 10, 50 or 100 of them safely.
“When you have higher complexity, your errors tend to multiply, and the predictability already goes out the window,” he said.
The technology, he added, is already ahead of “what we can do safely”.
William Tjhi, head of applied research at AI Singapore (AISG), said the most pressing talent gap is for “bilingual” engineers who know both a domain and AI. On a healthcare project, he found that it was not more AI engineers that would have sped things up, but AI engineers who understood healthcare. They also need what he called “domain safety” or “domain governance” – a sense of where to put human checks in an agentic workflow, and what to fall back on if an agent fails.
AISG, creator of the Sea-Lion family of open models for Southeast Asian languages, is expanding it with Nvidia’s Nemotron open models and NeMo tools. When asked if the region prefers bigger or smaller models, Tjhi said Sea-Lion’s Hugging Face downloads favoured smaller ones, but a large model such as Nemotron can help make them more capable through distillation.
AISG has openly released benchmarks and pipelines it built for Sea-Lion, and others have picked them up. During a recent visit to Lagos, Nigeria, Tjhi heard from an AI lab in Uganda that had taken AISG’s Sea-Helm evaluation pipeline and linguistic diagnostics and adapted them for Luganda, Swahili and other African languages, then extended them to voice, something AISG has yet to do.
“I think this kind of thing can only happen if it is open source,” he said.

articles.title: Nvidia Stock Set For 40% Surge: 3 Catalysts That Could Drive the Next Big Move
articles.text:
NVDA earns a BUY with a $310.20 target (~40% upside), driven by the Vera Rubin ramp and $500 billion in mobilized AI infrastructure capital.
AMD's trailing P/E of 211 dwarfs NVDA's 45, while AVGO's AI semiconductor revenue surged 221%, confirming the AI infrastructure wave underpinning NVDA's outlook.
My 24/7 Wall St. price target for NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) is $310.20, which implies 39.56% upside from the current $225.35 quote. I rate NVDA a buy with high conviction.
Three catalysts drive the call: the Vera Rubin production ramp, more than $500 billion in third-party AI infrastructure capital being mobilized through NVIDIA partners, and the opening chapter of physical AI across robotics and autonomous vehicles.
NVDA is up 21.11% year to date and 28.17% over the trailing year. Q2 fiscal 2027 delivered revenue of $96.22 billion, up 105.85% year over year, with non-GAAP EPS of $2.22 beating consensus by 6.29%. Data Center revenue hit $89.023 billion. Management guided Q3 to $108 billion.
Why Bulls See $353 or Higher
The bull-case one-year target is $353.54. Jensen Huang told investors NVIDIA can supply only 70% of demand, with fiscal 2028 growth pegged at approximately 70%. Vera Rubin ramps platform value per gigawatt from Blackwell's $25 billion to $40 billion.
Hyperscaler capex is expected to reach nearly 800 billion in 2026 and 1.3 trillion in 2027, a wave that also pulls in the power, cooling, and networking suppliers we profiled in a free report on seven AI infrastructure names that aren't chipmakers. Analyst sentiment shows 57 Buy or Strong Buy ratings against 2 Holds and 1 Sell.
The bear scenario bottoms at $261.39, still above current price. Real risks include supply commitments of $279 billion, guarantee obligations capped at $108.5 billion, and DSO extending to 60 days.
Q3 guidance excludes China Data Center compute revenue citing geopolitical uncertainty. Gross margins are expected to bottom in the 71% to 72% range in Q4 on memory cost inflation, recovering to 72% to 73% in fiscal 2028 as volumes scale.
Advanced Micro Devices ( NASDAQ:AMD ) posted Q2 fiscal 2026 revenue of $11.536 billion, up 50.11%, with Data Center up 107%. AMD trades at a trailing P/E of 211 versus NVDA's 45, making NVDA the cheaper name on growth per valuation dollar.
Broadcom ( NASDAQ:AVGO ) competes in custom AI ASICs and networking. Q3 fiscal 2026 revenue reached $29.591 billion, up 85.5%, with AI semiconductor revenue of $16.70 billion growing 221% year over year. Its acceleration validates NVDA's guided $108.0 billion quarter sits inside a real industry wave. The peer set makes $310.20 look reasonable.
I'd own NVDA at $225.35 with a 24/7 Wall St. price target of $310.20 and a buy rating at 90% confidence. Supply-constrained demand into a Vera Rubin ramp management calls the fastest in company history drives the call.
I'd stay a buyer if hyperscaler capex tracks toward 1.3 trillion in 2027. I'd step aside if memory pricing pushes gross margin below 71% or if China restrictions widen beyond the Data Center compute carve-out.
These projections assume NVIDIA executes on the Vera Rubin ramp and hyperscaler AI spending holds. Significant upside or downside could result from broader China market access, a major AI capex reset, or accelerated adoption of physical AI and robotics platforms.

articles.title: I'm Buying More Nvidia Stock Right Now. Here's Why.
articles.text:
Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) has grown into the world's largest company, with a market cap of more than $5 trillion. Its graphics processing units (GPUs) are the gold standard for training and running high-level computing and artificial intelligence programs.
Some people may, however, look at Nvidia's stock price and think that the shine is coming off Jensen Huang's company. Shares are up 21% so far this year, which is fine, but that's not even close to the 239% gain in 2023, the 171% jump in 2024, or even last year's 39% increase. Meanwhile, stocks like Sandisk , Micron , and Intel are all up more than 200% this year and have become Wall Street darlings.
Are Nvidia's best days in the rearview mirror? Absolutely not. While the chipmaker may not replicate its massive 2023 gain, Nvidia remains an incredibly profitable company whose growth story is far from over. In fact, I think Nvidia is going to be putting up some wild numbers in the next two or three years, and that's why I'll be buying more Nvidia shares .
Nvidia is still growing fast, despite its size
What stands out in Nvidia's most recent earnings report is that the company is still growing at a triple-digit rate. Revenue in the second quarter of fiscal 2027 (ending July 26, 2026) was $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year ago. Of that, $89 billion, or roughly 92.5% of the company's total revenue, came from its data center segment.
Net income was $59.68 billion, up 126% from a year ago, and earnings per share of $2.46 were up 128% from last year. Nvidia is very profitable -- its operating expenses totaled only $8.4 billion for the quarter, and its gross margin was an impressive 75%.
"We're the only company in the world that creates and builds, offers an entire AI factory platform, a full-stack system. And customers can still mix and match," CEO Jensen Huang said. "However, most companies just don't have the skills to do that or desire to do that. And so, there's an entire part of the market that we experience growth. There's sovereign AI, there're regional AIs, there're neoclouds, there're AI start-ups, there're enterprises, where we're seeing -- which represents about half of our business, and that's growing 100% a year."
Nvidia's new product line is just getting started
Nvidia's Hopper and Blackwell architectures have been enormously popular among hyperscalers and neoclouds building computing capacity to meet the growing demand for AI. But the company's Vera Rubin architecture, which uses NVLink chip-to-chip interconnects so its Rubin GPUs and Vera central processing units (CPUs) can share memory and improve efficiency, generates even more revenue. CFO Colette Kress said the Vera Rubin -- now in full production -- and full-stack AI platform has expanded the company's total addressable market from a range of $18 billion to $25 billion per gigawatt from Blackwell to $40 billion from Vera Rubin.
That's one of the reasons why Huang has been so confident in his prediction -- which he made last year and recently reiterated -- that AI infrastructure spending would reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030. And speaking to reporters last week while in Scotland, Huang suggested that Nvidia would double its chip sales in the coming year.
It's hard to get a group of people to agree on anything -- that's just human nature -- but Wall Street experts are nearly unanimous on Nvidia stock. Analysts at Rosenblatt have a "Buy" recommendation and a $390 price target, representing potential upside of 73%. Bernstein's analysts have a $400 price target and an "Outperform" rating, and Raymond James analysts have a whopping $515 price target and a "Strong Buy" rating.
Nvidia is expected to report another strong quarter when it next reports earnings (likely in late November), with the consensus revenue estimate of $109.0 billion, up 91.2% from the previous year. And more of the same is expected for next year, following the Vera Rubin ramp-up.

articles.title: Micron vs. NVIDIA: 1 AI Stock to Buy Now and 1 to Watch
articles.text:
Micron vs. NVIDIA: 1 AI Stock to Buy Now and 1 to Watch
Micron's Q3 revenues reached $41.46B, driven by strong demand for high-bandwidth memory chips.
NVIDIA's Data Center revenues surged 117% to $89B, while total revenues jumped 106% year over year.
NVIDIA's 63.7% net margin and 96% ROE exceed Micron's 55.9% and 72.5%, respectively.
The rising demand for memory and Data Center infrastructure amid the artificial intelligence (AI) boom benefited both Micron Technology ( MU Quick Quote MU - Free Report ) and NVIDIA Corporation ( NVDA Quick Quote NVDA - Free Report ) . Here is a look at how the two stocks compare after their latest earnings reports and which one presents a more compelling buying opportunity.
Strong HBM Demand Drives Micron’s Growth and Outlook
According to Micron’s June 24 press release, the company’s revenues for the fiscal third quarter of 2026 came in at $41.46 billion, significantly higher than $23.86 billion in the previous quarter and $9.3 billion recorded a year earlier.
The company’s top-line growth was driven by robust demand for Micron’s cutting-edge high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips. Demand for HBM, which is widely used in AI servers, remains strong due to its capability to competently manage complex AI workloads while offering improved power efficiency.
Looking ahead, Micron expects revenues to rise to around $50 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter of 2026. The company also projects a healthy gross margin of approximately 86%, supported by strong demand for AI-related memory products and favorable pricing.
Data Center Growth Drives NVDA’s Revenues and Profitability
NVIDIA’s Data Center segment remained its key growth driver, with revenues surging 117% year over year to $89 billion in the fiscal second quarter of 2027, according to the company’s Aug. 26 press release. Total revenues reached an exceptional $96 billion, representing a 106% year-over-year and 18% sequential jump.
Along with revenue growth, the company’s profitability has also strengthened. NVIDIA’s gross margin rose to 75% from 72.4% a year ago, while both GAAP and non-GAAP net income increased. NVIDIA’s GAAP operating income has more than doubled year over year, implying significant operating leverage.
Looking ahead, NVIDIA projects $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, in revenues for the fiscal third quarter of 2027, signaling continued sequential growth. Profitability is also expected to remain robust, and with the Vera Rubin platform entering full production, NVIDIA is well-poised to benefit from the next phase of demand for AI infrastructure.
Micron or NVIDIA: Which AI Stock Is a Better Buy Now?
Driven by strong HBM demand, Micron delivered strong revenue growth and profitability, while robust Data Center growth has boosted NVIDIA’s revenues and profitability. However, unlike Micron’s growth, which is much more concentrated in the memory cycle, NVIDIA’s broader AI infrastructure exposure gives the Jensen Huang-led company a stronger growth outlook and greater earnings visibility.
Additionally, NVIDIA’s 63.7% net profit margin, compared with Micron’s 55.9%, indicates greater efficiency in converting revenues into bottom-line profits.
Moreover, NVIDIA appears more efficient than Micron at generating profits from shareholders’ equity. This is because NVIDIA’s return on equity (ROE) of 96% exceeds Micron’s ROE of 72.5%.
Overall, NVIDIA’s broader AI exposure, stronger margins, and higher ROE make it a more compelling investment opportunity now than Micron. New investors may consider waiting for Micron’s upcoming earnings release on Sept. 30, after the market close, to assess growth and opportunity before making an informed investment decision.
NVIDIA currently has a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), while Micron has a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). You can see the complete list of today’s Zacks Rank #1 stocks here .

articles.title: What Could Stop NVIDIA Stock Over The Next Six Months?
articles.text:
What Could Stop NVIDIA Stock Over The Next Six Months?
NVIDIA (NVDA) stock has returned 32% over the past six months, well ahead of the S&P 500. That run began near the bottom of its worst fall of the past year. In August 2026, management said rising memory costs will cut NVIDIA’s gross margin, the share of sales kept after production costs. At $303 billion of sales over the past year, each margin point is worth about $3 billion. The table shows what could stall that run over the next six months and when each event lands.
now, and at least through the end of fiscal 2028
NVIDIA reports fiscal Q3 2027 results
NVIDIA’s Fiscal Q3 Report Lands On November 17
NVIDIA reports its fiscal Q3 2027 results after the market closes on November 17, 2026. Management has guided revenue to $108 billion , plus or minus 2%.
The company began production shipments of Vera Rubin, its newest data center system, in August 2026. Management expects Vera Rubin to bring in about 20% of data center revenue in fiscal Q3 2027. On November 17, watch whether revenue clears the low end of that guide, about $106 billion. The same report will show how gross margin held up against rising memory costs.
The Memory Costs Squeezing NVIDIA’s Margin
Management expects gross margin to hit its low in fiscal Q4 2027, at 71% to 72%. It was 75% in fiscal Q2 2027. Memory is the cause: management said memory prices rose more than it had expected.
NVIDIA has already set price increases that take effect in fiscal Q1 2028. Management expects those higher prices to lift margin to 72% to 73% in fiscal 2028. On November 17, watch fiscal Q3 2027 gross margin against 73.5%, the low end of management’s gross margin guide for that quarter. A reading below that would mean the margin is falling faster than management planned.
Higher prices can lift the margin off its low. They cannot add chips when the whole supply chain is already stretched.
Can NVIDIA’s Supply Chain Build Enough Chips?
NVIDIA cannot build enough for now. Management expects supply to stay a bottleneck at least through the end of fiscal 2028. On the fiscal Q2 2027 call, management said its entire supply chain is stretched.
Management’s preliminary outlook is for revenue to grow about 70% in fiscal 2028. Management called that outlook supply-constrained. Demand without that limit would be a lot higher, management said.
Management expects sales to the largest cloud companies to speed up again in fiscal Q4 2027, as Vera Rubin supply grows. On November 17, watch whether management keeps its fiscal 2028 growth outlook. A lower figure could mean tighter supply or softer demand. Note which one management names.
If you hold NVIDIA stock, you will hold it through all three of these events. The stock has fallen hard within the past year.
How Much NVIDIA Stock Can You Hold Through This?
Only as much as you could leave alone through a 20% drop, the stock’s worst fall in the past year . NVIDIA stock took that loss between October 29, 2025, and March 30, 2026. Over that fall, a $10,000 stake became about $7,980.
Report days add swings in both directions. NVIDIA stock gained 7.0% over the two days around the August 2026 earnings call. It lost 4.1% over the two days around the February 2026 earnings call.
If a loss of that size would push you to sell, your position is too large for these dates. Size it so a repeat of that fall is a loss you could sit through. NVIDIA needs its margin to stop where management said it would, and revenue to land near its guide.

items.quote: Three catalysts drive the call: the Vera Rubin production ramp, more than $500 billion in third-party AI infrastructure capital being mobilized through NVIDIA partners, and the opening chapter of physical AI across robotics and autonomous vehicles.

items.summary: The consensus revenue estimate for NVIDIA's next quarterly report (expected in late November) is $109.0 billion, up 91.2% from the previous year, with similar performance expected for the following year after the Vera Rubin ramp-up, according to the article.
items.quote: Nvidia is expected to report another strong quarter when it next reports earnings (likely in late November), with the consensus revenue estimate of $109.0 billion, up 91.2% from the previous year. And more of the same is expected for next year, following the Vera Rubin ramp-up.

items.summary: NVIDIA guided fiscal third-quarter 2027 revenue to $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, which the article describes as continued sequential growth, and said profitability is expected to remain robust.
items.quote: Looking ahead, NVIDIA projects $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, in revenues for the fiscal third quarter of 2027, signaling continued sequential growth. Profitability is also expected to remain robust, and with the Vera Rubin platform entering full production, NVIDIA is well-poised to benefit from the next phase of demand for AI infrastructure.

items.summary: NVIDIA management expects supply to remain a bottleneck at least through the end of fiscal 2028 and said on the fiscal Q2 2027 call that its entire supply chain is stretched.
items.quote: NVIDIA cannot build enough for now. Management expects supply to stay a bottleneck at least through the end of fiscal 2028. On the fiscal Q2 2027 call, management said its entire supply chain is stretched.
